prime.problem: At small batch a decode step spends almost all its time reading weights, so the GPU's math sits idle, and one run yields one token. Scoring several guessed tokens in one run would be almost free, but only if you can accept guesses without changing what the model would have sampled.
prime.fits: First speculative card. Course 2's speculative-sampling card gave the recipe and a batch-1 model; this one walks Leviathan et al.'s algorithm, proof and theorems in the paper's own notation.
expect: draft q, target p, accept with min(1, p/q)
resampling from the residual max(0, p − q)
acceptance α and Eq 1 (expected tokens per run)
prime.goal: Run one accept/reject decision by hand, prove to yourself that the output is exactly p, and compute expected tokens and speedup for any α, γ and c.

attend: Why does the paper only need to handle plain sampling, even though engines use top-k, top-p and temperature?
When the draft over-proposes a token, how often is it kept, and where does the rejected probability mass go?
Why does every target run produce at least one token and at most γ + 1?
What does Eq 1 assume about acceptances across positions, and how far off was it in the bigram toy?
Why does total arithmetic go up while memory reads per token go down, and when does that trade stop paying?

must: Draft proposes x ~ q → target keeps it with probability min(1, p/q) → on rejection sample from norm(max(0, p − q)) → accepted mass min(p, q) plus residual mass p − min(p, q) = p → the output is exactly the target's distribution for any draft and any sampling method

Target scores all γ + 1 positions in one run → each run yields accepted drafts plus one fix or bonus token → E = (1 − α^(γ+1)) ÷ (1 − α) tokens per run (3.36 at α = 0.8, γ = 4) → capped at 1 ÷ (1 − α)
Each iteration costs γ draft runs plus one target run → speedup = E ÷ (γc + 1) → a cheap draft (small c) is as important as a good one (high α) → at c = 0.66 even α = 0.867 gives about 1.1×
Rejected positions waste the target's math → total ops rise (1.55× at α = 0.8, γ = 4) while weight reads per token fall ÷ E → only pays while the step is memory-bound with idle math
elevated: Under argmax both p and q are one-hot → min(1, p/q) becomes 'accept if equal' → greedy speculative decoding is a special case, not a different algorithm
reference: Chen et al.'s swapped letters (q = target)
App A.2 comparison with one-shot rejection sampling

compress.prompt: From memory, write the one-token rule (accept, residual) and the A.1 identity that makes it exact. Then write Eq 1 and Theorem 3.8 and one sentence on what each input costs you.
checklist: accept with min(1, p(x)/q(x)); else sample from norm(max(0, p − q))
α = E[Σ min(p, q)] = 1 − E[total variation]
longer γ helps only while c is small and α high; the curve is flat near its best γ

retrieve.q: Explain why speculative sampling is exact for any draft model, and what the draft's quality affects instead.
answer: a token comes out either proposed-and-accepted (probability min(p, q)) or via the residual (p − min(p, q))
the two add to p(x) for every x, whatever q is
the draft only changes how often guesses are accepted, i.e. speed

retrieve.q: Trace one decision: p = (rug 0.45, sofa 0.25, mat 0.20, floor 0.10), q = (0.25, 0.15, 0.50, 0.10). The draft samples 'mat' and r = 0.71. What happens, and what is the residual distribution?
answer: keep probability min(1, 0.20/0.50) = 0.40; r = 0.71 > 0.40, so reject
residual max(0, p − q) = rug 0.20, sofa 0.10, others 0; its sum is 0.30 = 1 − β

retrieve.q: With α = 0.8 and c = 0.05, the best γ is 8 (3.09×) but γ = 4 already gets 2.80×. What argues for the shorter draft in a real engine?
answer: the curve is flat near its peak, so the extra 0.3× is small
longer drafts put more tokens into each verify pass, which eats idle compute sooner as batch grows
later draft tokens have lower acceptance in practice (acceptance isn't i.i.d.), so Eq 1 overestimates long γ

compare.q: Leviathan's rule and Medusa's typical acceptance both decide which draft tokens to keep. What does each guarantee about the output, which design choice causes the difference, and when is each the right call?
answer: Leviathan: exactly the target's distribution, via min(1, p/q) plus the residual
Medusa: accepts tokens above an entropy-scaled threshold, so more acceptances but not distribution-exact
use exact rules when outputs must match the model (evals, sampling-sensitive tasks); typical acceptance when speed matters more and quality is re-checked

compare.q: Course 2 modelled speculation on an H100 with a 1.0B draft (2.24× at batch 1). Which of this card's theorems does that model use, and which assumption of §3.3 does it test at large batch?
answer: it uses Eq 1 and the speedup form E ÷ (cost per iteration)
§3.3 assumes γ + 1 parallel target positions cost the same as one (memory-bound)
at large batch that fails: verify passes become compute-bound, and the gain falls to 1.26× at 128 and 0.70× at 256

predict.q: Corollary 3.9 says that if α > c, some γ gives at least (1 + α) ÷ (1 + c). For α = 0.7 and c = 0.1, what is that floor, what does γ = 3 give, and what is the best γ? Commit to numbers before revealing.
predict.answer: Floor (1.7) ÷ (1.1) = 1.55×. γ = 3: E = (1 − 0.7⁴) ÷ 0.3 = 2.53 tokens, cost 1.3, so 1.95×. Best γ is 4 at about 1.98× (our search over γ = 1…50), matching the card's table row for α = 0.7, c = 0.1. So the guarantee is loose, and γ = 3 is already within 2% of the best.

apply.task: Check exactness by hand for p = (A 0.5, B 0.3, C 0.2) and q = (A 0.2, B 0.3, C 0.5). Compute β, the residual distribution, and the final probability of each token (proposed-and-accepted plus rejected-then-residual). Then run labs/spec-sim.py and change the draft to something worse in the bigram toy: confirm that TV(output, p) stays at sampling-noise level while tokens per run fall.
apply.done: A three-row table (min(p, q), residual share, total) that sums to p exactly, and a note of the TV and tokens-per-run the lab printed for your worse draft.
apply.hint: Check the hand part after trying: β = 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.7; residual = (A 0.3, B 0, C 0) ÷ 0.3 = all on A; totals: A 0.2 + 0.3 × 1 = 0.5, B 0.3, C 0.2.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the Cor 3.9 floor, or how close γ = 3 is to the best?
Could you explain why the output is exact without writing any formula, in words about 'over-proposed' and 'under-proposed' tokens?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: α and γ → tokens per run, or c → cost per run → speedup?
What surprised you: that any draft is exact, or that a bigram draft still gives 1.25×?
Before Part II: which input, α or c, do you expect our Mac to get wrong?
